jobs.description_html: The newly founded Max Planck Institute for Political and Social Science studies contemporary challenges to political, social, and economic life. The institute places special emphasis on the political dimension, thereby spanning the spectrum from political sociology through conflict and peace research to political economy. Rigor and imagination guide the institute’s analytical and empirical approach, which draws inspiration from cross-disciplinary developments. The institute aims to produce new, evidence-based insights for pressing challenges to policy and contemporary society. At the Institute, the Department of Political Institutions and Conflict is inviting applications for the position of Doctoral Researcher (m/f/d) (full-time for three years with a starting date of January 1, 2027). The newly established department “Political Institutions and Conflict” (led by Ursula Daxecker) studies the relationship between political institutions and conflict, broadly construed. Conflict is inherent in politics but can be managed peacefully or break out in the open and turn violent. Research in the department explores whether and how political, economic, and social institutions create or reduce the potential for conflict, how structural changes have changed institutions’ ability to manage conflict, and how these shifts affect political outcomes downstream. Through this research, the department aims to produce novel insights for important challenges in contemporary society, including the rise of extreme strategies and violence, threats to electoral integrity, and democratic erosion. The PhD candidate will be affiliated with the “Doctoral Network Democratic Institutions and Violence Network in Europe (DIViNE)” project, funded by the HORIZON MSCA action. The candidate will be supervised by Dr. Ursula Daxecker. DIViNE brings together leading European research environments — UvA (Amsterdam), UESSEX (Essex), UMIL (Milan), UC3M (Carlos III de Madrid) and UU (Uppsala) — and partner organizations – including the new Max Planck Institute for Political and Social Science — to combine complementary strengths in quantitative conflict research, behavioral and experimental methods, historical and archival inquiry, institutional and normative theory, and applied policy engagement. Responsibilities (what you will do): Democracies are commonly seen as able to channel contestation through institutionalized processes and nonviolent action. Yet, democratic politics frequently experience a broad range of political violence — from riots and organized electoral intimidation to extremist mobilization and criminal violence — and violence can test and, at times, erode democratic norms and institutions. Moreover, democracies themselves may respond to perceived threats with measures (e.g., militarized policing, emergency legislation, selective repression) that threaten to undermine core features of liberal democracy such as the rule of law, civil liberties and institutional impartiality. The DIViNE Doctoral Network (Democratic Institutions and Violence Network in Europe) consolidates comparative, historical, theoretical and methodological strands to build a coherent new research program on political violence in democracies. The position is part of WP3 on Dynamics of Support for Violent Movements and Responses, which focuses on the micro-foundations of public support for, and tolerance of, political violence, including how violent organizations cultivate legitimacy. The PhD project aims to explain variation in violent strategies across time and space, distinguishing between violent rhetorical and behavioral strategies. The project is also interested in understanding the relationship between rhetoric and behavior, and how both strategies shape outcomes downstream. Empirically, the project examines political violence in the Global North, aiming to conduct subnational, constituency-level analyses of violent strategies in Global North cases. The methodological approach makes uses of innovations to study sensitive topics and difficult-to-reach populations, such as shadowing, fieldwork, special survey techniques, and use of multimodal data. The project will generate policy-relevant knowledge on patterns of radicalization, public tolerance for violence, and the vulnerabilities of established democracies. The doctoral trajectory includes a secondment at the University of Amsterdam and Clingendael in the Netherlands, which will provide the PhD candidate with additional training and exposure to policy engagement and strategic communication on extremist threats. Specifically, you will: produce a doctoral thesis that will be defended at the University of Amsterdam’s Faculty of Social Sciences, with the goal of obtaining the degree of PhD. conduct PhD research on the dynamics of support for violent movements and responses, including quantitative analysis of data, surveys and survey experiments, and fieldwork interviews. co-author publications with other project members; carry out fieldwork and interviews in research locations; assist with administrative responsibilities related to the project, such as the organization of workshops, conferences, or other project events. take active part in DIViNE training network activities including network training modules, PhD colloquia, research workshops, secondments, and training workshops; be affiliated with and take active part in the research environment at the department and institute. Regular physical presence at the Institute is therefore required and researchers need to reside within commuting distance of Göttingen. We will assist with finding adequate housing and with applying for visas and residence permits. Requirements: You have the following credentials: Essential: a Master’s degree or equivalent in political science or closely related discipline. The degree must have been obtained by the start of your employment; an excellent command of social science research methods, including quantitative methodology such as panel regression, analysis of large administrative data, survey data, large language models and AI, causal inference design, and statistical programming in Stata/R/etc.; excellent oral and written communication skills in English; independent thinking and critical analytical skills; the ability to work independently and in a team. Desirable: experience with qualitative methods and mixed-methods approaches; interest and willingness to conduct fieldwork; expertise in research on political violence. What We Offer: The position is full-time and for a period of three years (with the option of up to two extensions of six months each). Salary is based on the German collective agreement for civil servants (TVöD Bund), pay group EG 13, 75%/​grade 1 – 2. The Max Planck Society is mainly funded by German Federal and State Governments (see www.mpg.de). Max Planck Institutes provide outstanding facilities, academic resources and intellectual environments for the support of independent research. Max Planck Institutes are not tied to universities. There are no teaching obligations for staff, but teaching and other forms of co-operation with universities are possible. The Max Planck Society wishes to increase the participation of women across the sciences. Applications from women are therefore particularly welcome. Following its commitment to equal opportunities employment policies, the Max Planck Society especially encourages applications from persons with a disability. Persons of any nationality can apply. Applications must be submitted online no later than Wednesday, November 11, 2026. Applications must consist of: a CV a two-page cover letter that outlines your preparation and motivation to pursue this degree a two-page proposal outlining a PhD project that fits the above parameters unofficial undergraduate and graduate transcripts the contact details of two academic references a writing sample of max. 10 pages (this can be an excerpt from longer written material). The deadline for applications is November 11, 2026. Additional materials such as recommendation letters will be requested only for shortlisted candidates. The selection committee expects interviews to take place in Göttingen in the week of November 23. We ask you to ensure availability this week. Queries should be directed to silvia.stoermer@ips.mpg.de. The Institute has been newly reestablished in 2026. Apply now! Max Planck Institute for Political and Social Science Hermann-Föge-Weg 11 37073 Göttingen For information on the institute, please consult ips.mpg.de.

jobs.title: PhD Student Positions (f/m/x) Electron-Light Interaction in Silicon Photonic Nanostructures
jobs.description_html: At the Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences, we bridge the gap between basic research and technological advancement. Here, researchers from the fields of physics, chemistry, biology, and medicine collaborate across disciplines, supported by high-performance service facilities and a modern research infrastructure. As the largest institute of the Max Planck Society, with around 1,000 employees from more than 66 nations, we offer an inspiring, international working environment with exceptional scientific breadth. The Department of Ultrafast Dynamics (Prof. Dr. Claus Ropers) is inviting applications for two PhD Student Positions (f/m/x) – Electron-Light Interaction in Silicon Photonic Nanostructures – Study the interaction of free electrons with silicon nanostructures, including the investigation of quantum effects. Conduct scientific work at the emerging intersection of electron microscopy and quantum photonics. Primary emphasis is on ambitious experimental work using electron microscopes and silicon photonic structures. The MPI-NAT invites applications for two fully funded Marie Skłodowska-Curie Doctoral Candidate positions, within the Horizon Europe Doctoral Network QUEST – Quantum Electrodynamics with Silicon Nanotechnology (QuEST). QUEST brings together leading European universities, research institutes and innovative companies to advance quantum technologies through silicon nanotechnology. Within this network, you will be one of 15 doctoral candidates working on complementary research projects spanning semiconductor materials, nanofabrication, quantum photonics, quantum electrodynamics, advanced characterization and theoretical modelling. The two PhD candidates will conduct research in the above-mentioned scientific field, while focusing on different areas of specialization. Project 1 focuses on enhancing electron-light interactions in tailored nanostructures using flexible geometries and variable beam energies. Meanwhile, project 2 will explore hybrid devices that couple local quantum states to electron beams. One application applies to both projects simultaneously. If you have a preference, please indicate in your application which project interests you most. Candidates will be matched to a project based on qualifications, skills and their stated preference. Position details The selected PhD candidates will participate in the EU-funded HORIZON-MSCA-2025-DN project QUEST, combining network-wide training activities with excellent research opportunities at MPI-NAT. You will be expected to work on your project in close collaboration with fellow PhD students in QUEST and with the other members of the Department of Ultrafast Dynamics. Together, you will explore, experimentally and theoretically, novel custom photonic devices tailored for efficient interactions with electron beams and solid-state quantum systems. In particular, this includes assisting the design and optical coupling of photonic structures, performing extended experiments in an electron microscope and complementing the results with numerical simulations. You are expected to communicate your results in the form of scientific publications and presentations at international conferences. As part of the GAUSS PhD program at the University of Göttingen, you will complete several PhD courses and participate in teaching as a teaching assistant. You will also attend regular meetings with other PhD students and partners in the doctoral network, including two training schools and two workshops. The duration of the stay in Göttingen (Germany) and the two secondments vary by project as follows: Project 1 is set to last a total of 36 months, which includes two 2-month secondments each to Copenhagen (Denmark) and Göttingen (Germany). Project 2 includes a 32-month stay in Göttingen and two 2-month secondments each to Copenhagen (Denmark) and Dresden (Germany), so that this project is also scheduled to last a total of 36 months. For the respective secondments, you are expected to relocate to the project partners. Your profile The ideal candidates for the positions are highly motivated and talented researcher holding a Master’s degree (MSc or equivalent) in physics, chemistry, or engineering, with an excellent academic record and preferably demonstrated scientific achievements. We are interested in working with candidates who are team-minded, reliable, self-driven and have demonstrated excellence in electron microscopy, nano-optics, integrated photonics or quantum optics during their Master's thesis (or equivalent). Other qualities of the successful candidates: Is academically curious and thinks deeply and creatively Takes responsibility for the progress and quality of the project Communicates well in both written and spoken English Is empathetic and enjoys working with others from diverse backgrounds The positions are subject to the mobility and eligibility rules of the Marie Skłodowska-Curie actions. In particular, the candidates must not have resided or carried out their main activity (work, studies, etc.) in Germany for more than twelve months during the three years immediately prior to the recruitment date, unless as part of a procedure for obtaining refugee status under the Geneva Convention. At the date of recruitment, the candidates must be a Doctoral Candidate, i.e. in the first five years (full-time equivalent research experience) of their research career and must not have been awarded a doctoral degree. What we offer The successful candidates will receive a salary in accordance with the MSCA regulations for Doctoral Researchers. The salary includes a living allowance, a mobility allowance, and a family allowance (if applicable). The PhD funding is for 36 months. The two PhD positions are full-time with a 39-hour workweek and will start on 01/01/2027 or according to mutual agreement. We are committed to being a cosmopolitan institute that offers a diverse and inclusive working environment with equal opportunities. We also aim to increase the number of employees with disabilities. jobs.description_html:
The International Max Planck Research School for Ultrafast Imaging and Structural Dynamics in Hamburg, Germany, offers a structured PhD program focusing on ultra-fast phenomena, X-ray physics and dynamical imaging in all areas of science, covering physics, chemistry and biology. 23 Interdisciplinary doctoral PhD projects in the fields of Ultrafast Science and Quantum Materials Research The program offers exciting research opportunities at ultra-intense electron and X-ray sources to directly observe atomic motions during primary events. The use of ultrafast imaging over the relevant length and time scales generates new levels of understanding of the interplay between structure and dynamics. Specific areas include the theoretical and experimental aspects of quantum materials and atomically resolved dynamics, fundamental light-matter interaction, accelerator-based light sources, coherent controlled molecular and solid-state dynamics, molecular imaging, extreme timescale spectroscopy, ultrafast optics and X-ray science.

We offer:
  • A range of PhD positions in these areas: > open positions
  • State-of-the-art research facilities on an extensive science campus
  • Cross-disciplinary research in a vibrant, international scientific environment
  • First class supervision and mentorship by a team of internationally renowned experts
  • Outstanding training in your scientific subject and transferable skills (in English)
  • A 3-year employment contract based on the German federal pay agreement
Requirements We seek applicants with an excellent academic background. You hold (or are about to complete) an MSc degree or equivalent in physics, chemistry or related areas. You need to be passionate about research in ultrafast phenomena and motivated to conduct rigorous scientific work over the full degree period. Apply Applications must be submitted via the > online application portal.
The application deadline is 6th November 2026. PhD projects start in summer/​autumn 2027. In exceptional cases, it may be possible to start on the research project earlier. For any further questions or problems regarding the application process or the online system, please contact the IMPRS UFAST coordinator at
> IMPRS.UFAST@mpsd.mpg.de. › Apply now!

jobs.title: Doctoral Position in High Intensity Electron Sources for Future Accelerators
jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in High Intensity Electron Sources for Future Accelerators Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in High Intensity Electron Sources for Future Accelerators 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken Our research group, based at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI), explores new technologies for future accelerator facilities. Through the development of new technologies and techniques, we develop high intensity particle sources, high gradient particle accelerators and beam diagnostics systems that measure beam qualities down to the sub-femtosecond regime. Our research combines beam/plasma physics, unique RF technologies and high-power lasers to realise the accelerators that exist within the Paul Scherrer Institute and reaching beyond with contributions to CERN’s future circular collider (FCC). This Doctoral Position will be based at PSI Villigen but with teaching assistant duties at ETH Zurich. Project background The project involves developing electron sources for future accelerator facilities at PSI and the institute’s contributions to the FCC. A central shared challenge is shaping the electron beam as it is generated or shortly afterward. For the FCC, precise control of the laser profile in the RF photogun enables the flexible filling schemes needed for top-up operation. For X-ray free-electron lasers, like SwissFEL, transverse laser shaping and early RF compression are key to producing brighter electron beams. This PhD project will advance beam-shaping techniques for both applications. Job description Commission a new electron source test stand and demonstrate pulse-to-pulse modulation of bunch charge, beam size, and laser pulse energy relevant to the FCC-ee electron source concept Compare laser-shaping techniques through beam measurements, build a prototype for photocathode operation, and investigate machine-learning/AI-based optimization to improve performance Study photocathode and laser performance, including the lifetime of semiconductor photocathodes at bunch charges of up to 5 nC Measure gains in beam brightness from both photocathode laser shaping and RF compression with applications to a SwissFEL upgrade (SwissFEL+) Profile Master’s degree (or equivalent) in physics, accelerator science, electrical engineering, photonics, or a closely related field Strong interest in accelerator physics, electron sources and experimental work; experience with beam dynamics, lasers/optics, numerical modelling or scientific programming is an advantage A practical, independent and analytical working style, combined with enthusiasm for interdisciplinary collaboration Professional proficiency in English; knowledge of German is an asset Workplace Workplace We offer We are a dynamic, interdisciplinary research group committed to innovation and collaboration. As a Doctoral student with us, you will benefit from comprehensive on-the-job training alongside a wide range of personal and professional development opportunities. We are strongly committed to vocational training and to supporting your growth both as a scientist and as a professional. We value work-life balance and offer modern employment conditions with on-site infrastructure designed to give you the flexibility to accommodate your personal interests and family commitments. As part of our team, you will have access to: A stimulating research environment combining fundamental beam physics, laser physics, and RF technology development, with hands-on practical experience in designing, commissioning, and operating particle accelerators A broad range of transferable skills with applications in both academic research and industry State-of-the-art instruments and fully operational accelerator facilities Large-scale, multidisciplinary projects that build teamwork and collaboration competencies across a wide range of scientific and engineering interfaces Enrollment in the ETH Doctoral Programme Teaching and mentoring opportunities chevron_right Working, teaching and research at ETH Zurich We value diversity and sustainability In line with our values , ETH Zurich encourages an inclusive culture. jobs.title: Doctoral Researcher in Humanoid Robotics, 3D Perception and Embodied AI
jobs.description:
Doctoral Researcher in Humanoid Robotics, 3D Perception and Embodied AI Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Researcher in Humanoid Robotics, 3D Perception and Embodied AI 100%, Zurich print Drucken The Advanced Manufacturing Lab (am|z) at ETH Zurich, led by Prof. Markus Bambach, is seeking a highly motivated Doctoral Researcher to conduct research in humanoid robotics, 3D perception, and embodied artificial intelligence for autonomous manufacturing. The position is embedded in an interdisciplinary research project aiming to enable humanoid robots to perceive, understand, and interact with complex manufacturing environments using novel RGB-D sensing technologies. We are looking for a candidate with a strong background in robotics, computer vision, or machine learning who is passionate about developing intelligent robotic systems and translating scientific concepts into working solutions. The successful candidate will investigate novel approaches to robot perception, simulation-to-real transfer, and autonomous manipulation, contributing to the development of intelligent humanoid systems capable of performing complex manufacturing tasks. Project background The Advanced Manufacturing Lab at ETH Zurich investigates advanced robotic technologies for flexible, intelligent, and autonomous manufacturing. This Doctoral Researcher is part of a collaborative research project focused on developing intelligent humanoid robotic systems using next-generation, single-chip RGB-D sensing technologies. The project aims to integrate novel depth-sensing hardware with advanced perception algorithms, simulation environments, and learning-based robotic control to enable autonomous and collaborative manufacturing operations. Research activities span several interconnected areas: 3D simulation and synthetic data generation: Development of realistic manufacturing environments and simulation pipelines for generating annotated RGB-D data 3D semantic perception: Development of learning-based methods for object detection, segmentation, and scene understanding using RGB-D sensor information Sim-to-real transfer: Investigation of methods for transferring perception and manipulation capabilities from simulation to physical robotic systems Autonomous robotic manipulation: Integration of perception, planning, and control for robotic handling and assembly operations Collaborative humanoid robotics: Investigation of learning-based coordination strategies, including multi-agent reinforcement learning, for cooperative manufacturing tasks Language-guided robotic actions: Exploration of approaches that enable robots to interpret natural-language instructions and translate them into executable actions The project combines fundamental research with experimental validation using physical humanoid robotic platforms and real manufacturing scenarios. The doctoral research will focus on selected scientific challenges within these areas, with opportunities to contribute to the development of a fully integrated autonomous humanoid manufacturing demonstrator. Job description Conduct independent scientific research in humanoid robotics, 3D perception, and learning-based robotic systems Develop and evaluate novel algorithms for RGB-D-based object detection, semantic segmentation, and 3D scene understanding Design and implement realistic robotic simulation environments and synthetic data generation pipelines for manufacturing applications Develop methods for improving the transfer of perception and manipulation capabilities from simulation to real-world robotic systems Design and implement data acquisition, annotation, processing, and evaluation workflows for synthetic and real RGB-D datasets Integrate perception algorithms with robotic manipulation, motion planning, and control frameworks Investigate learning-based approaches to autonomous robotic decision-making, with opportunities to explore multi-agent coordination and language-guided manipulation Implement, test, and validate developed methods on physical robotic and humanoid platforms Plan and conduct scientific experiments, establish quantitative benchmarks, and systematically evaluate the performance of developed methods Develop reproducible research software and contribute to shared software frameworks and experimental infrastructure Publish research findings in leading international robotics, computer vision, and machine learning conferences and journals Collaborate with researchers and industrial partners involved in the project and contribute to the supervision of student research projects Profile We are looking for a highly motivated and independent researcher with strong analytical and programming skills, scientific curiosity, and a passion for intelligent robotic systems. You should have: A Master's degree in Robotics, Computer Science, Mechanical Engineering, Electrical Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, or a closely related field A strong foundation in robotics, experimentation, quantitative evaluation, and the analysis of experimental results Familiarity with Linux-based development environments, Git, and collaborative software development practices The ability to independently investigate challenging research questions, develop new ideas, and systematically evaluate potential solutions A strong motivation to pursue doctoral research and contribute to scientific publications Fluent English, both written and spoken Knowledge of Korean and/or German is an advantage The following qualifications would be an advantage: Experience with RGB-D cameras, depth sensing, point clouds, 3D reconstruction, or semantic scene understanding Familiarity with robotics frameworks such as ROS/ROS 2 Experience with robotics simulation platforms such as NVIDIA Isaac Sim, MuJoCo, Gazebo, or similar environments Experience with synthetic data generation, dataset annotation, or simulation-to-real transfer Knowledge of reinforcement learning, imitation learning, or learning-based robotic manipulation Familiarity with vision-language models (VLMs), large language models (LLMs), or language-conditioned robotic policies Experience with multi-robot systems, humanoid robotics, or collaborative manipulation Hands-on experience integrating sensors, programming robots, or conducting experiments on physical robotic platforms Familiarity with Docker, automated testing, CI/CD pipelines, or reproducible machine learning workflows Previous research experience demonstrated through a Master's thesis, research projects, publications, or contributions to scientific conferences We particularly encourage applications from candidates who combine strong theoretical foundations with practical programming skills and an interest in validating their research on real robotic systems. jobs.title: Doctoral Fellowships in Architecture and Technology
jobs.description:
Doctoral Fellowships in Architecture and Technology Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Fellowships in Architecture and Technology 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Architecture & Technology (A&T) Doctoral Programme is looking for exceptional candidates to join our group of 50+ international doctoral students. We are offering two paid, full-time (100%), 3.5-year doctoral fellowships to start on October 1, 2027 . Since its inauguration, 32 scholars have been granted an A&T Fellowship. Graduates of the programme have successfully obtained academic positions at leading research institutions worldwide and high-level positions in the industry. The programme provides funding for three and a half years. It offers excellent working conditions and a unique research infrastructure. You will be employed full-time and receive monthly salaries based on a standard rate . Please find the detailed information about the doctorate at ETH Zurich in the AVETH survival guide . Project background About the Programme The A&T Doctoral Programme is ETH Zurich’s interdisciplinary educational platform committed to training scholars in research and teaching of technology in architecture. The programme is offered and managed collaboratively by the chairs of the Institute of Technology in Architecture (ITA) . The work of the ITA chairs assimilates many diverse aspects of employing science, technology and engineering in architecture, including computational design of buildings and structures, building processes and systems, digital and robotic construction and fabrication, and many others. For more information about our institute, please consult the ITA website . The following professorships are currently involved in the A&T doctoral programme: Architecture and Digital Fabrication (Gramazio Kohler Research) Architecture and Structures (Block Research Group) Structural Design Digital Building Technologies (DBT) Architecture and Building Systems (A/S) Construction Heritage and Preservation Architecture and Human Augmentation You will join one of the above professorships under the respective professor/mentor. Hence, we expect you to choose one professorship most suitable for realising your research proposal and explicitly indicate this in your application packages. Although the selected applicant will be primarily associated with the chosen professorship, the interdisciplinary character of the programme ensures the involvement of other parties during the studies. For example, one of the milestones of this doctoral programme is the Aptitude Colloquium, in which doctoral students defend their research plan before all ITA professors and researchers. Our work takes place in the Arch_Tec_Lab , a high-tech zero-emissions building designed and developed by ITA. Job description We are looking for excellent people whose work demonstrates productive synergies between architecture and technology We welcome architects with a solid technical, engineering or scientific background or interests and engineers/scientists whose work relates to architecture We advise the applicants to thoroughly consult the ITA professorships’ websites before applying to ensure their research interests are compatible Profile You must hold a Master’s degree acquired at the university level in architecture, engineering or related fields (e.g., MSc, MEng or MArch) Upon successful admission, depending on the your academic background, the ETH administration office will evaluate if you need to take any additional exams at ETH during your first year of studies English is the official language, and we assume you are proficient in this language We do not formally require English language certificates as a part of the application package Workplace Workplace We offer Your job with impact: Become part of ETH Zurich, which not only supports your professional development, but also actively contributes to positive change in society You can expect numerous benefits , such as public transport season tickets and car sharing, a wide range of sports offered by the ASVZ , childcare and attractive pension benefits chevron_right Working, teaching and research at ETH Zurich We value diversity and sustainability In line with our values , ETH Zurich encourages an inclusive culture. We promote equality of opportunity, value diversity and nurture a working and learning environment in which the rights and dignity of all our staff and students are respected. Sustainability is a core value for us – we are consistently working towards a climate-neutral future . Curious? So are we. jobs.title: Doctoral Student in Glaciology and Glacial Hazards
jobs.description:
Doctoral Student in Glaciology and Glacial Hazards Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Student in Glaciology and Glacial Hazards 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken We are looking for a Doctoral Student to join the team of the Professorship of Glaciology for four years. Our group is affiliated with ETH’s Laboratory of Hydraulics, Hydrology and Glaciology (VAW) as well as the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research (WSL). Project background The Doctoral Student is offered within the project Stability of cold hanging glaciers under climate warming in the French and Swiss Alps (ICEFAL). ICEFAL is composed of a Swiss-French consortium studying the effects of rising ice temperatures on the stability of cold hanging glaciers and their likelihood to be the source of large ice avalanches. The overarching goal of the project is to provide a data-driven method to create an index of hazard potential for all hanging glaciers in the French and Swiss Alps, with applicability beyond the study region. The index combines geometric and thermal considerations. To achieve this goal, the project combines fieldwork, state-of-the-art thermo-mechanical modeling, and regional-scale geospatial analyses. Job description To achieve the project goals, the successful candidate will: Create an inventory of hanging glaciers using manual mapping and possibly machine-learning aided approaches Perform field measurements at high-elevation sites in Switzerland The goal is to  collect measurements of ice temperatures, which will be complemented with mass balance measurements, firn cores, and analyses of long-term ice-avalanche monitoring data Leverage the collected field data as well as available meteorological data to drive a state-of-the-art thermo-mechanical model (Elmer/Ice) to investigate the past and future evolution of the temperature field of the investigated glaciers and possible repercussions on stability Predict basal temperatures of hanging glaciers from approaches developed at VAW-Glaciology and by project partners, and intersect these with stability criteria to derive a hazard index for hanging glaciers in the study region The work will be supported by postdoctoral and senior researchers of VAW-Glaciology and is based in Zurich. Profile The successful candidate brings a combination of the following skills and experiences to the project: Required : A Master’s degree in geophysics, physics, environmental or earth science, environmental engineering, or related fields Excellent knowledge of English, both in oral and written form (C1 to C2) Desired background and interest in the following topics: A keen interest in high-mountain hazards A solid foundation in math and physics Glaciologic training or expertise A willingness to conduct fieldwork in a high-mountain environment Geospatial analysis and processing skills (e.g., QGIS) Experience with hazard and risk management concepts Prior experience with physics-based numerical modeling Familiarity with a scripting language (e.g.,  Python or Matlab) Outdoor or mountaineering experiences Interest and experience working in teams Knowledge of German and/or French We stress that successful applicants do not need to come with all desired skills/experiences. Furthermore, candidates with non-traditional academic backgrounds are strongly encouraged to apply. Workplace Workplace We offer We are a dynamic and international research group, fully dedicated to the study of glaciers, ice sheets and the impacts resulting from their changes. We value a welcoming, friendly, and supportive working atmosphere and strive for excellence in all we do. The working languages in our group are English, (Swiss) German, French, and Italian. For more information on our group and activities, please visit the following website and/or our social media channels (@VAW_glaciology). chevron_right Working, teaching and research at ETH Zurich We value diversity and sustainability In line with our values , ETH Zurich encourages an inclusive culture. jobs.title: Doctoral Position in Risk-Based Inspection and Maintenance Planning of Tunnels
jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in Risk-Based Inspection and Maintenance Planning of Tunnels Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in Risk-Based Inspection and Maintenance Planning of Tunnels 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Chair of Infrastructure Management, led by Professor Dr. Bryan T. Adey within the Institute of Construction and Infrastructure Management of the Department of Civil, Environmental and Geomatic Engineering, has an opening for a doctoral student. This position focuses risk-based inspection and maintenance planning for tunnels, including probabilistic risk updating, Value of Information analysis, and intervention program optimisation. This position is part of an interdisciplinary SNSF project in collaboration with the Free University of Bozen-Bolzano, the Hagerbach Test Gallery, and the EuroTube Foundation. The preferred starting date is 1 February 2027, although other dates are negotiable. Project background Tunnels are critical links in transport networks, and many Swiss road and rail tunnels are ageing while being subject to increasing traffic loads, climate-related stressors, and evolving safety requirements. Their maintenance involves two interdependent asset domains, namely structural elements, such as lining, portals, and drainage, and mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems, such as ventilation, lighting, and fire detection. In current practice, these domains are managed largely in isolation, inspections remain heavily manual, and evidence from different campaigns, sensors, and specialists is fragmented across separate reports and databases. Interventions are therefore often planned using disjointed evidence and conservative heuristics, even where substantial data exist. The project Predictive, Resilient, Integrated Systems for Management of Tunnel (PRISM-T), funded by the SNSF, addresses this challenge through an integrated digital twin workflow for tunnel maintenance decision support. Heterogeneous inspection and monitoring evidence is transformed into uncertainty-aware condition indicators, which are used to update risk, to assess whether additional information is worth collecting, and to derive executable intervention programs. Extended reality (XR) is used to validate decisions and to guide inspection and maintenance work on site. The workflow is developed and validated in the Tunnel Digitalisation Centre of the Hagerbach Test Gallery in Flums, and its transferability is tested at the DemoTube facility of the EuroTube Foundation in Dübendorf. Regular field work at both sites and close collaboration with the partner team in Bolzano form an integral part of the doctoral research. Within this project, the doctoral position addresses the decision layer of the workflow, in which maintenance decision processes are formalised and uncertainty-aware condition indicators, developed in a companion doctoral position, are used to update risk and to optimise intervention programs under realistic tunnel constraints. Job description The successful candidate will map and formalise current tunnel maintenance decision processes for the structural and mechanical, electrical, and plumbing domains through workshops and interviews with practitioners. On this basis, risk and consequence models based on Bayesian networks will be formulated, and incremental risk updating methods will be developed. A computationally tractable Value of Information analysis will be developed using approximation strategies, such as surrogate models and scenario reduction. Intervention program optimisation models accounting for sequencing, bundling, access windows, and resource constraints will be formulated and solved, with outputs traceable to the underlying evidence. The candidate will contribute to validation campaigns at the Hagerbach Test Gallery and the EuroTube Foundation. jobs.description:
Doctoral Researcher in Pulse Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Researcher in Pulse Electron Paramagnetic Resonance 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Spin Dynamics and Hyperpolarisation group is looking for a doctoral researcher, fully funded by a Starting Grant from the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF). The group explores ways to enhance the sensitivity of electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR, also known as electron spin resonance, ESR) by orders of magnitude. The project lies at the interface between method development and applied chemical spectroscopy. Starting date: by mutual agreement. There is no deadline and the position will remain open until suitable candidates are found. Applications are considered as long as this advertisement is online. Job description The position involves working with a state-of-the-art pulse EPR spectrometer with arbitrary phase and amplitude control. The aim is to develop new pulse sequences with improved sensitivity and higher information content, and to apply them to challenging systems from inorganic chemistry and catalysis, as well as to organic radicals. Our group is also developing a new method based on optical hyperpolarisation, which will eventually be applied to the same systems. The work will focus on the spectroscopic aspects, including experiments and spin-dynamics simulations. Depending on the candidate's background, it can also include chemical synthesis and catalysis, as well as quantum-chemical calculations. The working language of the group is English. Profile The candidate must hold a Master's degree in (physical) chemistry or a related field by the start of the position. Interest in spin dynamics, magnetic resonance, and their applications to (in)organic chemistry is essential. Research experience in an advanced magnetic resonance technique (EPR, solid-state NMR, or similar) is required. A good understanding of the physics underlying magnetic resonance is expected. In addition, the candidate should have: the drive to take ownership of their project and push it forward openness to collaborating with people from different backgrounds Workplace Workplace We offer An exciting project at the forefront of magnetic resonance method development A position in a new research group with close collaboration and structured mentoring Considerable freedom to pursue your own ideas and to develop both academically and personally World-class infrastructure Opportunities to initiate your own collaborations chevron_right Working, teaching and research at ETH Zurich We value diversity and sustainability In line with our values , ETH Zurich encourages an inclusive culture. We study liquid-like light in fast-gain semiconductor lasers, where strong nonlinear dynamics can produce stable and controllable broadband states. Our research combines semiconductor device fabrication, precision optical experiments, and theoretical and numerical modelling to understand and control these systems. Project background This project investigates the dynamics, fluctuations, and open-system physics of liquid light . The doctoral student will work across the full experimental cycle: developing and fabricating photonic devices, building and operating optical setups, performing precision measurements, and modelling the underlying nonlinear dynamics. Job description Designing and fabricating semiconductor photonic devices using cleanroom processes, followed by their electrical and optical characterization. Building and operating advanced laser and optical measurement setups to study temporal dynamics, fluctuations, coherence, and controlled light–matter interactions. Developing theoretical and numerical models to describe nonlinear laser dynamics, interpret experiments, and guide the design of new devices and measurements. The goal is to establish a versatile experimental platform for probing and controlling liquid-light dynamics, connecting device physics, precision measurements, and nonlinear photonic theory. Profile Strong background in physics and\or electrical engineering, photonics, or a closely related field. Interest in combining fabrication, experimental work, and theory/simulations. Advantage to previous experience with cleanroom fabrication, optical experiments, lasers, or numerical modelling is helpful, but specific platform experience is not required. jobs.title: RobotX PhD Fellowship 2027
jobs.description:
RobotX PhD Fellowship 2027 Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht RobotX PhD Fellowship 2027 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken RobotX, the Center for Robotics at ETH Zurich, is looking for outstanding doctoral students who want to build robots that work in the real world. With the RobotX PhD Fellowship 2027, you apply once and are considered by several RobotX research groups across ETH Zurich. You choose up to three professors you would like to work with, and they review your application. Application deadline: 27 November 2026. Job description The research groups of RobotX cover a broad spectrum of robotics, including but not limited to: Soft and Musculoskeletal Robotics: bioinspired robots built from compliant materials, artificial muscles, and tendons, for safe and adaptive interaction with an unstructured world. Robotic Locomotion and Manipulation: legged robots, robot arms, and hands that move and act reliably in complex terrain and contact-rich tasks. Biohybrid Robots: robots built from living cells, engineered tissue, and synthetic materials, actuated by muscle and powered by chemical energy. Perception and Computer Vision: 3D reconstruction, object recognition, and scene understanding that give robots reliable perception of their surroundings. Human-Robot Interaction: sensory-motor interaction between humans and machines for assistive, rehabilitative, and cooperative tasks. Computational Design and Fabrication: simulation, optimization, and learned surrogate models to design and fabricate efficient, bioinspired robots. Reinforcement Learning and Machine Learning: data-driven methods that let robots learn new skills and adapt to new tasks and environments. Humanoid Robotics and Tactile Sensing for Manipulation: humanoid loco-manipulation, whole-body control, and tactile sensing that let robots reason across touch and vision to handle objects dexterously. Motion Planning and Control: algorithms for navigation, control, and decision-making in dynamic environments. Safety-Critical Robotic Systems: robots that perform reliably under uncertainty, in particular when they work alongside humans. You define your doctoral project together with your supervisor during your first months. jobs.title: PhD Position in Experimental Nonlinear Dynamics and Nanomechanics
jobs.description:
PhD Position in Experimental Nonlinear Dynamics and Nanomechanics Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht PhD Position in Experimental Nonlinear Dynamics and Nanomechanics 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken We are looking for a highly motivated PhD student to join our nonlinear dynamics team. Do you have a broad interest in physics and technology? Do you like the prospect of working in an experimental project in close collaboration with theory? Are you creative, persevering, independent, and a good team player? You can expect a cutting-edge research project that is very challenging due to the many aspects of science that are involved. For the same reason, it is a highly rewarding experience if you enjoy expanding your knowledge beyond textbook physics. We look forward to meeting you! Project background Is it possible to build artificial neural networks from driven nonlinear resonators? This question builds on the ideas of Hopfield and Hinton, but takes them out of equilibrium: in our resonators, a balance of continuous drive and dissipation sustains stable oscillation states. This gives us access to phenomena that are absent in equilibrium physics. For example, this may allow us to investigate how a physical network turns stored memories into dynamical patterns. In our lab, each node is an electrical circuit or a micro-electromechanical (MEMS) resonator implementing a Kerr parametric oscillator (KPO): a driven, dissipative resonator with two stable oscillation states that act like a bit of memory. We couple several such KPOs, reading out every oscillator simultaneously and in real time. This gives us complete access to the dynamical many-body phase space. With it, we reconstruct the attractor landscape of the network, track how noise drives switching between collective states, and measure probability currents that appear when detailed balance is broken. The central question is whether these currents organize into stable, reproducible temporal patterns and coexisting limit cycles. Networks like these bridge nonequilibrium statistical physics and neuromorphic computing, and could provide a physical route to Ising and Boltzmann machines that operate on dynamical rather than static states. Job description Build and operate a programmable network of coupled KPOs with up to eight nodes, including control and readout electronics and measurement software. Map attractor landscapes, switching statistics and probability currents from measured trajectories. Compare experiment with simulations and analytical models in close contact with our theory partners (Prof. O. Zilberberg at the University of Konstanz) and publish and present your results internationally. Profile You hold (or are about to complete) an MSc in physics, electrical engineering or a related field, with a solid background in nanomechanics, nonlinear dynamics, or statistical physics. You enjoy hands-on experimental work (electronics, signal processing, Python) and are not afraid of a bit of analytical theory. Experience with MEMS, lock-in detection, or FPGAs is a plus. You communicate well in English. jobs.description:
Doctoral position in cognitive and moral heuristics in lay people’s reactions to climate change adaptation Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral position in cognitive and moral heuristics in lay people’s reactions to climate change adaptation 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken We are looking for a motivated doctoral student who is interested in applying psychological concepts and methodologies to environmental topics. The position is available starting January 2027. Project background While climate change mitigation (e.g., reduction of greenhouse gas emissions) remains important, it is also clear that societies need to adapt to the unavoidable hazards associated with climate change. The recent heat waves in Europe and the health and economical damages they caused, exemplify that adaptation measures are not yet sufficiently in place. Heuristics (mental shortcuts) can bias people’s risk perceptions and affect moral considerations. As such they can influence people’s private adaptation behaviors and their perceptions of technologies that could help societies to deal better with the consequences of climate change. By influencing regulations, they can also impact the exposure of vulnerable groups to hazards, such as heat. The aim of this doctoral thesis is to gain insights in how cognitive and moral heuristics influence the effective implementation of climate change adaptation measures. jobs.title: PhD Position in Atmospheric Chemistry
jobs.description:
PhD Position in Atmospheric Chemistry Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht PhD Position in Atmospheric Chemistry 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Atmospheric Chemistry group at the Institute for Atmospheric and Climate Science (IAC) – ETH Zurich invites applications for a 4-year PhD position on “Investigating oxidized nitrogen in the troposphere”. The Atmospheric Chemistry group at ETH conducts research exploring the processes controlling tropospheric composition (gases and particles) and their intersection with global change. Research makes extensive use of global modeling tools (GEOS-Chem and CESM) and analysis of large observational datasets. Nitrogen oxides (NOx) emitted into the troposphere contribute to the formation of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and ozone (O3). NOx thus plays a central role in global air quality and climate. Despite this key role, the complex cycling of NOx with other forms of oxidized nitrogen in the troposphere is not well constrained. Our growing understanding of sources and chemical transformations are not yet well represented or tested in large-scale models. The goals of this PhD project will be to better represent these processes in a global 3D model, to test resulting simulations against airborne, surface, and satellite observations, and finally, to investigate how changing NOx emissions have altered the cycling and impacts of tropospheric NOx over time. Job description Develop skills in atmospheric chemistry, global modeling, and data analysis of field observations. jobs.title: Doctoral Position in contact mechanics of architected interfaces
jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in contact mechanics of architected interfaces Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in contact mechanics of architected interfaces 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken At the Professorship of Solid Mechanics (SMEC) in the Institute for Building Materials at ETH Zurich, we aim to understand how materials deform, degrade, break, and ultimately fail. Our research is driven by curiosity about the physical mechanisms that underlie failure and by the ambition to translate this understanding into more reliable and resilient materials and structures. By combining numerical modeling, laboratory experiments, and theoretical analyses, we seek to link microscopic processes with the macroscopic behavior of both engineering and natural systems and develop predictive tools for mechanical failure. Our team is highly interdisciplinary and international, bringing together researchers with backgrounds in materials science, mechanics, and applied physics. We work across a broad range of topics, including the mechanics of particle systems (colloidal and granular), architected and topologically interlocked materials, the mechanics of fragility in collagen, the mechanics of earthquakes, fracture of soft materials, and modeling failure in multiphysical processes such as corrosion-driven degradation of concrete. What unites these efforts is a shared curiosity about why complex materials fail and a commitment to developing new concepts, experiments, and models that advance our understanding of failure mechanics. We are seeking a motivated and innovative doctoral student with a strong interest in solid mechanics, interface mechanics, and computational modeling to investigate how local contact interactions in architected materials shape their macroscopic interface response. The project will explore how architecture influences collective contact behavior, aiming to develop design principles. The work will combine physics-based numerical modeling, theoretical reasoning, and concepts from rough-surface and multiscale mechanics. Job description You will conduct a computational and theoretical investigation of how local contact interactions in architected materials collectively determine their macroscopic interface response. The work will connect cell-scale mechanics with concepts from multiscale/rough-surface contact mechanics to develop effective descriptions of architected interfaces. You will develop and use numerical models of lattice materials to investigate the underlying principles of contact behavior of architected materials. You will analyze how architectural features, material properties, and characteristic length scales influence quantities such as contact area, pressure distributions, interface stiffness, and load transmission. Building on these results, you will seek statistical or homogenized descriptions that connect the mechanics of individual contacting cells to the effective behavior of large architected interfaces. The position provides a stimulating environment for scientific growth and collaboration. Profile You hold an MSc degree in mechanics, physics, (civil, mechanical, aerospace, or bio-) engineering, material science, computational science, or a related discipline. You have a background in mechanics, applied physics, computational mechanics, scientific computing, or a related field. A foundation in areas such as solid mechanics, contact mechanics, or multiscale modeling is particularly relevant. You have experience implementing scientific code and assessing computational results through validation, verification, and quantitative comparison with reference data. You have prior programming experience in Python and have used version control. You are curious, self-motivated, and interested in using modeling and quantitative reasoning to answer mechanics and physics questions. Experience with architected materials, rough-surface contact mechanics, homogenization, statistical mechanics, or multiscale methods is an advantage but is not required; the project-specific methods and concepts can be learned during the doctoral studies. You are fluent in English (oral and written). You enjoy working in a team, possess the necessary social skills and communication abilities, and contribute proactively to a positive group atmosphere. jobs.description:
Doctoral Student in High-throughput Analysis of Protein-Protein Interactions Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Student in High-throughput Analysis of Protein-Protein Interactions 100%, Basel, fixed-term print Drucken The Nash Lab (Lab for Engineering Synthetic Systems) is jointly affiliated with the Department of Chemistry at the University of Basel and the Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering of ETH Zurich (located in Basel). We work at the interface of protein engineering, molecular biophysics, and synthetic biology, developing new experimental and computational approaches to understand and engineer proteins for useful biomedical and industrial applications. Our research combines high-throughput screening, directed evolution, and single-molecule biophysical methods, and spans projects from fundamental protein science to translational applications. Project background Many proteins in the human body experience shear stress and other types of mechanical force, and this is believed to play a central role in their activity. Yet we still lack high-throughput techniques to measure how proteins respond to mechanical force. This project will develop high-throughput methods involving molecular surface display and deep sequencing to study force-dependent behavior in protein systems. These datasets will, in turn, be used to train machine learning models capable of predicting mechanical behaviors of molecular and cellular systems. As a proof of concept, we will apply this platform to study interactions central to blood clotting, with direct relevance to Von Willebrand disease, a common bleeding disorder. The Doctoral Student will work at the interface of protein engineering, single-molecule biophysics, and machine learning, in close collaboration with a computational biology group (Beerenwinkel) at D-BSSE. The project offers hands-on training across the full pipeline, from high-throughput experimental design to predictive modeling, and the resulting methods and datasets are intended to serve as an open resource for the broader research community. jobs.title: Doctoral Student in Neuromotor Interfaces for Dexterous Robot Teleoperation (multimodal egocentric vision + EMG)
jobs.description:
Doctoral Student in Neuromotor Interfaces for Dexterous Robot Teleoperation (multimodal egocentric vision + EMG) Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Student in Neuromotor Interfaces for Dexterous Robot Teleoperation (multimodal egocentric vision + EMG) 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab invites applications for a fully funded PhD position at ETH Zürich at the intersection of robotics, wearable sensing, signal processing, machine learning, and human-computer interaction. The goal of this PhD is to develop neuromotor interfaces for dexterous robot teleoperation using two sensing modalities: 1) surface electromyography (sEMG) measured at the wrist or forearm, with the aim of decoding subtle hand and finger activity, continuous movement, and motor intent in real time. 2) egocentric vision as a complementary input channel. While EMG provides information about human motor intent, egocentric cameras can provide context about the surrounding scene, manipulated objects, hand–object interactions, and task state. Combining these modalities creates opportunities for interfaces that understand both what the user intends to do and what is happening in the environment. The PhD will focus on the computational and sensing methods required to make such systems robust, generalizable, and effective in real interactive settings, including multimodal learning and reasoning across neuromotor and egocentric visual signals , while exploring applications in Mixed Reality and other interactive systems. Particularly beneficial: You have a background in (or experience with) prototyping sensing systems ( embedded systems , signal acquisition, processing, PCBs) Note: This is not a position in biomedical engineering and there is no health focus. Project background Wearable EMG provides a direct and unobtrusive way to sense muscle activity underlying hand and finger movements. This creates opportunities for interfaces that can recognize subtle actions, continuously estimate movement, and infer motor intent before or without large observable movements. Making such interfaces work reliably outside controlled settings remains a substantial research problem. EMG varies across users and recording sessions and is sensitive to electrode placement, contact conditions, movement, and other sources of noise. This motivates research in signal processing, temporal machine learning, representation learning, adaptation, and real-time inference. A second challenge is that neuromotor signals alone provide limited information about what the user is interacting with and why a particular movement is occurring. The project will therefore combine EMG with egocentric vision to capture objects, hands, contacts, affordances, and task state. This creates a multimodal research problem: learning representations that combine neuromotor and visual information and developing methods for reasoning about human intent, hand–object interaction, and the state of an ongoing manipulation task. For robotic teleoperation, these multimodal signals can support systems that jointly reason about what action the user intends, which object or target the action refers to, and how that intent should be translated to a robot with a different embodiment. Relevant problems include dexterous manipulation, shared autonomy, multimodal intent inference, and reasoning over sequences of human and robot actions. Job description Develop signal-processing and machine-learning methods for multichannel EMG, including discrete and continuous decoding of hand and finger activity Develop egocentric computer-vision methods for understanding hands, objects, hand–object interactions, contacts, affordances, and task state Develop multimodal learning and reasoning methods that combine EMG with egocentric vision to infer motor intent and interaction context Investigate reasoning over objects, actions, interaction sequences, and task state to resolve ambiguous motor signals and anticipate intended actions Apply methods to dexterous robot teleoperation , including mapping human motor intent to robot manipulators and dexterous hands optionally: Prototype wearable sensing systems , including electrode configurations, signal acquisition, embedded processing, and hardware and software integration (huge plus) Develop and evaluate applications in robotics, Mixed Reality , and other interactive systems and as in each PhD Disseminate your findings in publications at top-tier venues and open-source research results and tools where appropriate Present research findings at academic conferences, workshops, and seminars Profile ETH requirements: written and spoken fluency in English an excellent master's degree (MSc., M.Eng. or equivalent) in Computer Science, Electrical Engineering, Robotics, or related field You bring: A strong foundation in machine learning , including classification and regression, model evaluation, representation learning, and generalization A solid understanding of signals and time-series data (e.g., sampling, frequency, phase, noise, spectral representations, and filtering) Strong programming skills and experience implementing and quantitatively evaluating computational methods An interest in building real-time sensing and interactive systems , including experimentation with physical sensors A strong background in one or more of the following areas is particularly beneficial: Electrical engineering and signal processing: EMG or other electrophysiological signals, sensor systems, embedded systems, electronics, or wearable sensing Robotics: manipulation, dexterous manipulation, teleoperation, robot learning, shared autonomy, or human-robot interaction Computer Vision: egocentric vision, hand and object pose estimation, hand–object interaction, contact and affordance estimation, video understanding, or action recognition Machine learning: temporal modeling, representation learning, multimodal learning, multimodal reasoning , domain adaptation, or learning from noisy sensor data Interactive systems: HCI, Mixed Reality, wearable computing, or real-time input systems We do not expect applicants to already be experts across all of these areas. You will have the opportunity to develop complete research systems spanning wearable sensing, egocentric perception, machine learning, and robotic interaction . In our research, we frequently collaborate with other groups and departments as well as institutions and companies in Switzerland and abroad. During your PhD, you will have the opportunity to contribute to and collaborate with the ETH AI Center and engage in ETHAR, ETH's Research Hub for Augmented Reality in collaboration with Google XR . The position provides access to infrastructure for wearable and embedded prototyping, egocentric sensing, interactive systems, and robotic manipulation. jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in neutral-atom quantum computing Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in neutral-atom quantum computing 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The newly established Atom Quantum Processing (AQP) group , led by Prof. Konrad Viebahn, at the Institute for Quantum Electronics within the Physics Department (D-PHYS), ETH Zurich, is seeking a highly motivated Doctoral Candidate. Our research focusses on ultracold neutral atoms and their application in quantum technologies, in particular, quantum computing. We are currently establishing a new laboratory for laser cooling, trapping, and imaging ultracold rubidium atoms in optical lattices. With newly developed methods, such as high-fidelity collisional atom-atom interactions, we build highly coherent quantum machines capable of creating massively entangled quantum states for computing, simulation, sensing, and metrology. Project background Neutral atoms are one of the most promising quantum architectures of today. Yet, the current roadmaps towards neutral-atom fault-tolerant quantum computers are almost exclusively based on Rydberg interactions in optical tweezers. While Rydberg-based gates are fast, they have a massive drawback: finite Rydberg lifetimes and unavoidable decoherence due to spontaneous emission. Instead, our research will employ collisional interactions between atomic qubits, which are highly coherent, passively stable, and very scalable. By using optical lattices instead of optical tweezers we can trap and control more qubits per given laser power, eventually leading to a scalability advantage over the neutral-atom state-of-the-art. We have recently overcome an important bottleneck in optical-lattice-based quantum processors, by integrating topological pumping as a method to shuttle atoms between lattice sites (see publications ). When combined with stable collisional gates, a new quantum architecture emerges with the ability to create massively entangled states, large-scale quantum simulation, quantum sensing and, eventually, fault-tolerant computing. In this experimental Doctoral project, you will play a central role in setting up the experimental apparatus, building a closely-knit team, and developing new concepts in collisional quantum processing. Job description Building up the AQP team in a collaborative, enthusiastic, and communicative environment Setting up laser system for laser cooling, trapping, and imaging of rubidium-85 atoms Engineering and assembling UHV (ultra-high vacuum) system with excellent optical access for the quantum processor Programming and integrating experimental control hardware (ARTIQ) for running quantum information experiments Investigating novel schemes for quantum information processing based on collisional interactions, including theoretical calculations and numerical simulations Preseting your results at scientific conferences and publishing your work Profile You should hold (or be close to completing) an MSc degree in physics, quantum engineering, electrical engineering, or closely related discipline You should have a strong motivation to build a quantum computer from scratch Excellent spoken and written English Willingness to work in an international and diverse team Experience in any of the following laboratory techniques would be advantageous: Fibre coupling Optical/fluorescence microscopy Doppler-free absorption spectroscopy Spatial light modulation Laser locking, optical resonators Optical interferometers Gaussian beam profiling CAD development Soldering PCB development FPGA development Digital signal processing (DSP) Workplace Workplace We offer We offer a stimulating doctoral project on quantum computing with state-of-the-art neutral-atom techniques. The successful candidate with join a collaborative and international research group and will receive training in experimental techniques for AMO and quantum optics.
